newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia set to announce forest jobs plan.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia set to announce forest jobs plan.

text.p: British Columbia will announce on Thursday an accord with forestry companies aimed at increasing employment in the sector by 21,000 jobs over the next four years.
After months of negotiations with forestry industry executives, Premier Glen Clark called a news conference in the northern community of Prince George to make the announcement.
"It's the biggest announcement I've ever been involved in," he said. "It's the biggest job creation program in Canadian history."

Following the announcement, Clark plans to tour forest communities where he is expected to sell the accord and blast a Greenpeace campaign aimed at persuading U.S. companies to stop buying lumber from British Columbia's old-growth forests.
The premier has long complained that British Columbia does not generate as many jobs as U.S. states from the timber it cuts.
Clark has threatened to take away harvesting rights from companies who do not meet the targets.

In exchange for boosting jobs, forestry companies like giant MacMillan Bloedel Ltd have called for regulatory relief and a reduction in their operating costs. Seventeen companies are signing on the accord, Clark has said.
The province recently granted one of the industry's wishes by streamlining logging regulations and has discussed lowering some stumpage fees, primarily on pulp logs.
But it must tread cautiously in changing stumpage and royalty fees for fear of raising trade tensions with the United States.

British Columbia raised stumpage fees two years ago in response to U.S. accusations they represented an unfair subsidy to Canadian producers and Canada signed a lumber trade deal with its neighbor to the south only a year ago.

Under an early draft of the jobs-timber accord, 7,500 new jobs would be created by the big lumber companies. Remanufacturing, which produces items like doors and other finished products, would have to create 5,000 jobs.
Forest Renewal, a government agency designed to revitalize the forest sector, would add 5,000 jobs in silviculture and environmental restoration.
Employment in the forest sector has been shrinking as the industry has suffered from weak pulp prices and lagging profitability. The sector lost 5,500 jobs last year.
The Vancouver Sun newspaper reported this week that the accord would entail direct industry jobs growth of only 10,500 with the rest coming from silviculture.

The accord also encourages workers to refuse overtime work to prod companies into adding staff. The newspaper said the province would also announce approval of a MacMillan Bloedel power project at its Port Alberni mill.
